title: “THERE IS A WAY THAT SEEMS RIGHT TO A MAN…” — THE TERRIFYING DANGER OF TRUSTING WHAT FEELS RIGHT
paragraphs: “THERE IS A WAY THAT SEEMS RIGHT TO A MAN…” — THE TERRIFYING DANGER OF TRUSTING WHAT FEELS RIGHT
The most dangerous road may not look evil. It may feel peaceful, reasonable, justified—even blessed. And that is exactly why Scripture warns us about it.
There are decisions you regret because you knew they were wrong when you made them.
And then there are decisions that frighten you years later because, at the time, they felt completely right.
Every door seemed to be opening.
You told yourself, “Surely God wouldn’t let me feel this strongly if this weren’t His will.”
And then somewhere down the road, everything began falling apart.
Not because Scripture stopped being true.
But because there is something the Bible has been warning humanity about for thousands of years:
That sentence should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because one of the most dangerous lies of our generation is also one of the most comforting:
God never told you that your heart was qualified to be your god.
And the book of Proverbs gives us a warning so serious that Scripture records essentially the same proverb twice, in Proverbs 14:12 and Proverbs 16:25:
Yesh derekh yashar lifnei-ish, ve’acharitah darkhei-mavet.
There is a way that is right before a man…
but its end is the ways of death.
Look carefully at what God does not say.
He does not merely warn about a way that looks wicked.
He warns about a way that appears יָשָׁר — yashar.
That is what makes this verse terrifying.
The road does not necessarily have a skull painted on the entrance.
Sometimes it even feels like peace.
Maybe you stayed in something because leaving felt cruel.
Maybe you entered a relationship because loneliness hurt more than compromise did.
Maybe you walked away from someone because your anger felt justified.
Maybe you withheld forgiveness because what they did really was terrible.
Maybe you kept the secret because telling the truth threatened everything you had built.
Maybe you called cowardice “protecting my peace.”
Maybe you called disobedience “following my heart.”
Maybe you even found people who would agree with you.
That is the frightening thing about deception.
If deception felt like deception, very few people would embrace it.
Deception succeeds because falsehood can feel true.
The first great human rebellion in Genesis did not begin because Eve looked at the forbidden fruit and thought, “I want destruction.”
Something that seemed capable of making her wise.
The serpent did not need to convince humanity to hate goodness.
He only needed humanity to redefine goodness apart from God.
And we have been doing it ever since.
But real feelings are not necessarily reliable authorities.
None of that means those feelings should sit on the throne.
Feelings can tell you something is happening inside you.
They cannot, by themselves, tell you what is holy.
Jeremiah 17:9 describes the human heart with uncomfortable honesty:
The heart is deceitful above all.
That does not mean every emotion you experience is sinful.
It means fallen human beings cannot safely treat inner desire as an infallible compass.
We need the Word of God.
Because Christianity is not the story of good people learning to trust themselves more.
It is the story of lost people being rescued by Someone they desperately needed.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your instincts.
And perhaps this is where the knife turns.
Because sometimes what “feels right” is exactly what keeps us from repentance.
Repentance has never depended on whether confession feels comfortable.
Forgiving someone may not feel fair.
Walking away from sin may not feel liberating at first.
Ending an ungodly relationship may feel like your heart is being ripped apart.
Confessing what you have hidden may feel terrifying.
Returning what does not belong to you may feel humiliating.
Apologizing when your pride has built an entire courtroom proving you were justified may feel unbearable.
Obeying God sometimes hurts before it heals.
Jesus told His disciples that He would suffer, be killed, and rise again.
Peter did what probably felt loving.
Surely protecting Jesus was the right thing.
Surely suffering could not be God's plan.
Surely preventing the cross was compassionate.
Yet Peter's human reasoning collided with the redemptive purpose of God.
and in the same moment oppose the road Jesus had come to walk.
That should humble every Christian who has ever said, “But I have peace about it.”
But “I feel peaceful” is not a replacement for “It is written.”
But none of them outrank the revealed character and Word of God.
Sometimes an open door is simply an open door.
Jonah found a ship going exactly where he wanted to go while running from what God had commanded him to do.
And emotional relief is not always the peace of Christ.
There are moments when obedience will cost you the very thing your flesh is begging you to keep.
And then there is Jesus in Gethsemane.
This is where our shallow definition of “follow your heart” collapses.
And in the anguish of Gethsemane, He prayed in submission to the Father’s will.
Jesus did not teach us that holiness means doing whatever feels easiest.
The road that looked like defeat became the road of victory.
God turned it into the place where grace was proclaimed to sinners.
And suddenly the entire story changed.
Jesus does not merely make bad people behave better.
He takes stories people thought were permanently ruined and writes grace across pages soaked in shame.
That is why you cannot build your life on what merely seems right.
You need the One who is right.
Jesus did not say, “Discover whatever path feels true to you.”
“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”
The Christian faith is radically Christ-centered because salvation is not found by looking deeper into ourselves until we discover our own truth.
And perhaps you are reading this with something already burning in your conscience.
Nobody else needs to know for this moment to matter.
That private justification you keep rehearsing because somewhere beneath all the excuses you already know what obedience would require.
Maybe you have been asking God to approve something He has already addressed.
Maybe you have been asking for another sign because you do not like the answer Scripture already gave you.
Maybe you have confused God's patience with God's permission.
Maybe you have spent months trying to make peace with something the Holy Spirit keeps bringing into the light.
Conviction is not God throwing you away.
Conviction may be mercy calling you home.
The man who had promised loyalty collapsed under pressure.
Imagine the shame when the rooster crowed.
There are moments when your worst sentence echoes louder than every good thing you have ever done.
Something you wish you could erase.
A season when you hardly recognize the person you became.
But Peter’s failure was not the final chapter.
Grace met the man who had failed.
That does not make sin insignificant.
The Gospel never says your rebellion did not matter.
The Gospel says it mattered so much that the Son of God went to the cross—and His grace is so great that repentant sinners can be forgiven, reconciled, cleansed, and made new.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.
Not by telling us to trust ourselves.
But by meeting sinners in truth and mercy and calling us:
Maybe this article is not asking you to discover whether you are a “good person.”
Maybe the deeper question is simpler:
Who has the final word in your life?
Because sooner or later every disciple reaches a crossroads where feelings and faithfulness stop walking in the same direction.
That moment reveals who sits on the throne.
So before you make that decision…
before you return to that relationship…
before you walk away from your marriage…
before you call something good merely because it feels good…
Pray without demanding that God agree with the conclusion you have already chosen.
“Lord, am I asking You to lead me—or am I asking You to bless where I already decided to go?”
That question can change a life.
And if something has already been exposed in you while reading this, do not run from Jesus.
There is mercy at the feet of Christ.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is cleansing for the ashamed.
There is restoration for the fallen.
There is no sin made safe by hiding it, but there is no repentant sinner who needs to fear that Christ's mercy is too small.
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose scars no longer get the final word.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody you know may currently be standing on a road that feels absolutely right.
They may be praying for confirmation when what they really need is truth.
They may never tell you they needed this.
Because there may come a night when what God says and what you feel seem impossibly far apart, and you will need the reminder again:
Sincerity does not make a road safe.
But hear this clearly, because biblical integrity matters more than a conversion:
It does not purchase God's favor.
It is not a substitute for obedience to Christ.
And we should not tell you that it automatically replaces whatever convictions you hold concerning tithes, offerings, or giving through your local church.
Scripture teaches generosity, but Scripture also protects believers from religious manipulation.
“ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ … μὴ … ἐξ ἀνάγκης”
Each one according as he has purposed in his heart … not under compulsion.
Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through spiritual pressure.
Do it because you genuinely believe this work is worth supporting.
Do it as voluntary support for Gospel-centered content, discipleship resources, and the continued expansion of material intended to point people toward Jesus Christ.
Your support helps us keep writing.
And support is not only financial.
Jesus is calling you to follow Him.
The deepest danger was never simply choosing the wrong career, dating the wrong person, sending the wrong message, or taking the wrong opportunity.
The deepest danger is building an entire life around a compass that cannot save you.
Your heart was never meant to be your Savior.
So when your feelings say one thing and Christ says another…
when culture applauds what Scripture warns against…
when everybody around you says, “Do what makes you happy”…
There is a way that seems right to a man.
And remember the Savior who calls you onto a better road.
But if it leads you deeper into obedience to Jesus, you are not losing your life.
You are learning where life is found.
Because one day, you may look back and realize that the moment God interrupted the road that “felt right”…
was the moment grace kept you from reaching its end.
Sometimes the mercy of God sounds like a roadblock because He can see the grave your feelings cannot.
